proposals.before: In Long'an 4 (AD 400), he claimed the imperial title at the southern suburban altar, issued a general amnesty, inaugurated the Jianping era, established a traveling ancestral temple south of the palace, and sent envoys bearing the accession proclamation.
proposals.after: In Long'an 4 (AD 400), at the southern suburb he assumed the imperial throne—an act the history presents as usurpation—issued a general amnesty, adopted the Jianping era name, established a temporary ancestral temple south of the palace, and sent envoys with a document to report the accomplishment there.
proposals.reason: Revise to restore the locative 焉, read as the immediately preceding temporary temple; this antecedent is plausible but interpretative. Attribute the evaluative 僭 to the history, not objective fact. Keep the document and reported accomplishment unspecified. The AD conversion in the idiomatic field remains unaudited.

proposals.before: Later at a banquet for his ministers, when the wine was warm he laughed and said, 'Though I am meager, I reverently face south to court the lords; not proud on high, anxious at my post by night; with whom among the ancients may I be compared?'
proposals.after: Later at a banquet for his ministers, when the wine was warm he laughed and said, 'Though I am meager, I conduct myself respectfully, face south, and receive the lords at court; not proud on high, anxious at my post by night; with whom among the ancients may I be compared?'
proposals.reason: 恭己南面而朝諸侯 depicts the south-facing ruler receiving the lords at court, not him courting them; the remaining inherited wording is not assessed by this focused repair.

proposals.before: He opened ironworks on Mount Shang and salt monopolies at Wuchang Marsh to swell the army's coffers.
proposals.after: He established smelting works on Mount Shang and a salt office at Wuchang Marsh to increase resources for the army and the state.
proposals.reason: The source specifies smelting and a salt administration for military and state use, but not iron, monopolies, or army coffers.

proposals.before: A eunuch helped Murong De over the wall into hiding.
proposals.after: Palace attendant Xun Jin helped De over the wall, and De hid at Jin's residence.
proposals.reason: 遜進 is the personal name Xun Jin; 進舍 is his residence. The subject of the second clause is rendered as De, without inventing Xun Jin as the agent of hiding.

proposals.before: Palace attendant Xun Jin helped De over the wall and hid him in a forward lodging.
proposals.after: Palace attendant Xun Jin helped De over the wall, and De hid at Jin's residence.

proposals.before: Duan Hong and the rest heard the alarm and sealed the four gates with troops.
proposals.after: Duan Hong and the others heard of the palace disturbance and stationed their troops at the four gates.
proposals.reason: The source places troops at the four gates but does not say they were sealed. 勒兵 also suggests mustering or commanding troops; this narrow correction does not resolve that nuance.

proposals.before: Murong De re-entered the palace, executed Hou Chimei's faction, and Murong Da fled to Wei.
proposals.after: Murong De entered the palace and executed Hou Chimei and the others; Murong Da fled in fear to Wei.
proposals.reason: 赤眉等 means Chimei and others, not necessarily a faction; 達懼 expressly gives Da’s fear. Names follow the immediately preceding context.

proposals.before: Sui replied, 'King Wu of Zhou closed Bi Gan's tomb, Han's Gaozu sacrificed at Lord Xinling's grave—both fixed their hearts on worthies and often cherished old deeds.
proposals.after: Sui replied, 'King Wu of Zhou raised a mound over Bi Gan's tomb, Han's Gaozu sacrificed at Lord Xinling's grave—both fixed their hearts on worthies and often cherished old deeds.
proposals.reason: In 武王封比干之墓, the transmitted gloss 積土為封 explains heaping earth over the tomb; “closed” wrongly suggests sealing the tomb rather than the commemorative mound action.

proposals.before: Spanning several thousand li, hosts exceeding a hundred thousand, we could west merge with strong Qin and north resist Great Wei.
proposals.after: Spanning several thousand li with a host exceeding a hundred thousand, we could annex strong Qin to the west and resist Great Wei to the north.
proposals.reason: 西並強秦 describes annexing Qin, not merging with it by agreement.

proposals.before: He staged a review west of the city with hundreds of thousands on parade.
proposals.after: He reviewed his forces west of the city: 370,000 infantry, 17,000 vehicles, and 53,000 armored cavalry. They stretched across the mountains and marshes, their banners filled the landscape, and the sound of gongs and drums shook heaven and earth.
proposals.reason: Restore the reported troop and vehicle figures and visual and sound details; these are the text’s figures, not an independently verified count. Vehicles avoids deciding the exact type of 車.

proposals.before: De climbed high and looked over them, and said to Liu Gui and Gao Yazhi, 'Formerly Xi Ke avenged Qi, Wu Zixu resented Chu, and in the end they could vent their fierce integrity and their names flow a thousand years.
proposals.after: De climbed high and looked over them, and said to Liu Gui and Gao Yazhi, 'Formerly Xi Ke took vengeance on Qi, Wu Zixu resented Chu, and in the end they could vent their fierce integrity and their names flow a thousand years.
proposals.reason: 仇齊 makes Qi the object of Xi Ke’s hostility, not the injured party whom he avenged. Other wording remains for separate review.

proposals.before: Thereupon he issued an edict making Chao crown prince, amnestied the realm, and for sons continuing fathers raised each man's rank two grades.
proposals.after: Thereupon he issued an edict making Chao crown prince and granting an amnesty throughout the realm; sons succeeding their fathers were each granted two grades of rank.
proposals.reason: The rank grant does not require a prior rank; match the independently revised idiomatic field without asserting an increase.

proposals.before: They ran decoy coffers out each gate and hid his true burial in the hills.
proposals.after: That night they prepared more than ten coffins and sent them out through the four gates, burying him secretly in the mountain valleys; in the end, no one knew where his body lay.
proposals.reason: 棺 means coffins, not coffers; preserve the number, nocturnal setting and uncertain location. The text does not explicitly identify any particular coffin as a decoy.

proposals.before: His temple posthumous title was Emperor Xianwu.
proposals.after: His posthumous title was Emperor Xianwu, a title this history treats as illegitimate.
proposals.reason: 諡 is the posthumous designation, not a temple name. 偽 expresses this history's claim of illegitimacy; the proposed 'Jin historian' risks misidentifying the compiler's period. Zizhi Tongjian 114 separately distinguishes 諡獻武皇帝 from 廟號世宗.

proposals.before: He was posthumously titled Emperor Xianwu.
proposals.after: His posthumous title was Emperor Xianwu, a title this history treats as illegitimate.
proposals.reason: 偽 expresses the source's judgment of illegitimacy, while 諡 is a posthumous title. Avoid 'the Jin historian': the Book of Jin is a later compilation, so that label misleadingly suggests an author from the Jin period. The wording attributes the judgment to this history rather than endorsing it.

proposals.before: He founded an academy with two hundred students from elite families.
proposals.after: He established educational offices and chose 200 students for the Imperial Academy from among the sons and younger brothers of officials from dukes and ministers on down, and young men from scholar families of the second rank.
proposals.reason: The Chinese distinguishes descendants of dukes, ministers and officials below them from a second group, scholar families of the second rank. It selects two hundred students across the groups. The rank qualifies the family in the second group. Liang Ruixue discusses this sentence explicitly on PDF page 30.

proposals.before: He established schools, selecting two hundred sons of dukes and ministers down to second rank gentry households as academy students.
proposals.after: He established educational offices and selected two hundred from among the sons and younger brothers of the dukes and ministers and those below them, and from scholar families of the second rank, to be students at the Imperial Academy.
proposals.reason: The Chinese distinguishes descendants of dukes, ministers and officials below them from a second group, scholar families of the second rank. It selects two hundred students across the groups. The rank qualifies the family in the second group. Liang Ruixue discusses this sentence explicitly on PDF page 30.

proposals.before: De said, 'I am now scattering the wealth I lightly esteem to recruit the deaths I heavily value; how could I be stingy for a revered kinsman?
proposals.after: De said, 'I am giving away wealth, which I value little, to enlist a man willing to die in my service, which I value greatly. How could I begrudge such a gift for a revered parent?
proposals.reason: Du Hong has offered to risk death on his mission and asked for a stipend for his father. 散所輕之財 and 招所重之死 contrast wealth that De readily gives away with the willingness to die that he prizes. 親尊 is left as a revered parent without supplying a possessor. The quotation continues in s0195.
